name: service-mesh
context: Large-scale distributed systems requiring uniform service-to-service communication, security, and observability across many microservices
benefits: mTLS encryption between all services with automatic certificate rotation
Comprehensive observability with metrics, logs, and distributed tracing
Built-in resilience patterns (circuit breakers, retries, timeouts, bulkheads)
Advanced traffic management (canary deployments, blue-green deployments, traffic splitting)
Zero-trust security model with fine-grained authorization policies
Developer productivity through transparent networking concerns
Consistent policy enforcement across all services
tradeoffs: Added infrastructure complexity and operational overhead
Sidecar proxy memory overhead (50-100MB per pod for Istio, 10-20MB for Linkerd)
Additional latency per hop (2-5ms typical, varies with configuration)
Steep learning curve for configuration and debugging
Resource consumption for control plane at scale
Potential for proxy configuration errors to cascade
use_cases: Microservices architectures with 15+ services requiring consistent policies
Multi-team environments needing namespace-level isolation and quotas
Organizations requiring compliance (PCI-DSS, HIPAA, SOC2) with audit trails
Teams needing canary or progressive delivery workflows
Environments requiring mTLS between all service communications
Multi-cluster or multi-region deployments needing consistent traffic management
Organizations migrating from monolith to microservices
avoid_when: Fewer than 10-15 microservices (operational overhead exceeds benefits)
Resource-constrained environments where memory overhead is unacceptable
Extreme low-latency requirements where even 2-5ms extra is problematic
Simple architectures where basic Kubernetes networking suffices
Greenfield projects that could use Linkerd's simpler approach initially
component_types: Sidecar Proxy: Per-pod proxy (Envoy/Linkerd) intercepting all network traffic, handling load balancing, circuit breaking, retries
Control Plane: Central management (Istiod/Linkerd controller) for proxy configuration, certificate authority, policy enforcement
Service Discovery: Automatic registration and endpoint location for service-to-service communication
mTLS Manager: Certificate generation, rotation, and mutual TLS enforcement between services
Circuit Breaker: Prevents cascade failures by detecting unhealthy services and ejecting them from load balancing pools
Observability: Metrics (Prometheus), distributed tracing (Jaeger), service graph visualization (Kiali)
Traffic Manager: Route rules, VirtualServices, DestinationRules for traffic splitting and canary deployments
Rate Limiter: Token bucket or rate limit policies to protect services from traffic spikes
Auth Policy: Authorization policies for zero-trust deny-by-default access control
anti_patterns: Distributed monolith (using mesh without proper service boundaries)
Mesh configuration sprawl (too many VirtualServices, DestinationRules)
Overly permissive authorization policies defeating zero-trust
Retry storms (missing perTryTimeout causing exponential retry amplification)
Ignoring sidecar resource limits causing OOM or CPU throttling
Deploying to production without namespace-level testing
design_principles: Zero-Trust Security: Never trust, always verify. All service-to-service communication requires authentication and authorization regardless of network location.
Incremental Adoption: Start with permissive mode, measure baseline metrics, and gradually enforce policies namespace by namespace.
Deterministic Traffic: Make traffic behavior explicit through configured subsets, route rules, and weighted routing to avoid accidental routing changes.
GitOps Configuration: Manage service mesh custom resources (VirtualServices, DestinationRules, AuthorizationPolicies) as code with version control.
Minimalism: Favor fewer, larger clusters to reduce control-plane complexity. Use namespace-level policies over individual pod configurations at scale.
Certificate Hygiene: Use short-lived workload certificates with automated rotation and metric-driven expiration alerts.
Observable Operations: Monitor not just applications but the mesh components themselves. Establish SLO-driven dashboards for latency, request volume, and error ratio.
Failure as First Class: Design for failure with circuit breakers, retries, timeouts, and fault injection testing before production.
best_practices: Start with permissive mode and gradually tighten security policies
Use namespace-level configurations to manage complexity at scale
Implement circuit breakers to prevent cascade failures
Enable automatic mTLS with short-lived certificates
Monitor both application and mesh component metrics
Use GitOps for managing mesh configuration
Conduct chaos engineering tests before production
Establish SLO-driven dashboards for latency, request volume, and error ratio
